US President Donald Trump meets South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in Gyeongju, South Korea, in 2025 [File: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters]By Joseph StepanskyPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
United States President Donald Trump will attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, where he is expected to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and hold a three-way meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
A Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of the economic summit, which includes 21 Pacific Rim member economies, would be the third time the two superpower leaders have met this year.

The prior meetings – with Xi hosting Trump in Beijing in May and Trump hosting Xi at the White House in September – were heavy on ceremonial pomp, as both leaders sought to portray a sense of stability in the consequential relationship, but light on meaningful breakthroughs.
Experts predicted a similar approach in Shenzhen, as topics of AI regulation, trade and the self-ruling island of Taiwan will again loom large.
The summit comes just days after Democrats won commanding control of both chambers of the US Congress, a shift that will likely serve as a major check on the US president in his final two years in office. Beijing, meanwhile, is increasingly looking beyond the Trump era to see what comes next.

A C-130 Hercules aircraft flies over the National Mall during Independence Day events in Washington, DC [File: Rahmat Gul/AP Photo]By AFP and The Associated PressPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.
Smashed every gauge in the cockpit
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.
According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft.
He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit. Advertisement

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announces charges related to an attack on a rideshare driver during a news conference in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on Tuesday [Ellen Schmidt/AP Photo]By AP and ReutersPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
A 25-year-old man has been charged in Minnesota with attempted murder and carjacking after an attack on a Somali-American Uber driver that prosecutors describe as “incredibly brutal”.
Mohamed Yusuf suffered broken ribs, a broken leg, spinal injuries, collapsed lungs and significant internal bleeding after being strangled with a seatbelt and run over by his own car in the city of Hopkins early on Saturday, according to court documents. His family said he was in a coma.

She said her office had charged Samit Apurva Patel with one count of second-degree attempted murder and one count of first-degree carjacking for the assault on Yusuf on November 14. Patel was taken into custody on Saturday.
Yusuf’s family claimed the attack was driven by hate, while civil rights advocates demanded a hate crime investigation.
Prosecutors said the evidence could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Patel’s behaviour was motivated by bias, though that “does not diminish the pain that the family and the Somali community is feeling right now”, Moriarty said.

The United States-backed Board of Peace has delivered a grim assessment to the United Nations Security Council, warning diplomats of conditions that threaten the year-old truce in war-torn Gaza.
In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board cautioned that, without immediate steps to implement the 2025 ceasefire deal, the truce between Israel and Hamas may be on the brink of collapse.

“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, which The Associated Press obtained.
The Board of Peace was created in 2025, at US President Donald Trump’s behest, to oversee the ceasefire deal and reconstruction in Gaza.
Since October 2023, the narrow coastal territory has been the target of a genocidal war carried out by Israel, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.
‘Cannot be sustained indefinitely’
In recent weeks, Israel has continued to carry out deadly air strikes, and its ongoing restrictions have prevented the delivery of life-saving aid into Gaza ahead of the winter season.
“Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts,” the board said in its report.

A group of fishermen from Ecuador have sued the administration of United States President Donald Trump over a drone strike that sank their vessel and injured members of their crew in March.
The lawsuit, filed on Monday in a Pennsylvania federal court, seeks financial restitution and any additional relief the court considers just.

It also petitions the court to issue an order ending the Trump administration’s campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
The complaint centres on the March 17 sinking of the fishing boat La Negra Francisca Duarte II, based in Ecuador.
“We filed the lawsuit because the boat was all we had. Nobody in Ecuador is helping us,” the ship’s captain, Hernan Flores, told the Reuters news agency. “They did all that damage to us, and by the grace of God, we’re alive.”
The government has not claimed responsibility for the strikes on La Negra Francisca Duarte II and two other Ecuadorian vessels that were attacked and sunk in recent months.
A report from the Washington Post in August, however, suggested that the vessels were targeted by the CIA as part of a secret overseas mission.

Residents of Bukavu in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to face the consequences of renewed fighting, displacement and violence despite diplomatic efforts to end the conflict [Al Jazeera]By Al Jazeera staffPublished On 18 Nov 202618 Nov 2026
Bukavu, DRC – For residents of eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the succession of diplomatic initiatives meant to end years of conflict is becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile with the violence unfolding around them.
In North and South Kivu provinces, fighting between the Congolese army and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), an armed and political coalition led by former President Joseph Kabila, has continued despite international efforts to secure a settlement. Civilians remain exposed to attacks, displacement and the disruption of essential services.
The latest escalation has raised questions about whether negotiations in Washington and Doha can deliver security on the ground, and whether the separate diplomatic efforts are sufficiently coordinated to make progress.
“One meeting follows another, and they all end up being much the same,” said Blaise Chasumba, a resident of Bukavu, the provincial capital of South Kivu. “But the real peace that the warring parties are dangling before us is far from becoming a reality on the ground. We continue to lose our loved ones and our homes.”
A conflict with deep historical roots
The Washington Accords, signed in December 2025, seek to address tensions between the DRC and neighbouring Rwanda. The commander of the Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Esmail Qaani, has arrived in Iraq to push for a solution amid simmering tensions near the town of Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of the pro-Iranian armed group Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi official has told Al Jazeera.
The Iraqi official explained that Qaani met with Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and held meetings with forces within the Coordination Framework—an umbrella for Shia Iraqi parties in the Iraqi parliament—in an effort to reach an agreement amid rising tensions over an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.

Iraq recently launched a sweeping anti-corruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.
While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, some analysts say they believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of pro-Iranian armed groups that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.
